title: Respiration (Aerobic & Anaerobic)
description: How cells release energy from glucose — aerobic and anaerobic respiration, the role of mitochondria, muscle fatigue, and respiration in plants and yeast.

notes.heading: What is Respiration?
notes.body: Respiration is NOT the same as breathing (ventilation). Respiration is a chemical reaction that occurs inside every living cell, releasing energy from glucose. It is an exothermic reaction — it releases energy in the form of ATP (adenosine triphosphate), which powers all cell activities. All organisms respire continuously — plants, animals, fungi, and bacteria. The energy released is used for: muscle contraction (movement), active transport (moving substances against concentration gradients), building large molecules from smaller ones (protein synthesis, DNA replication), cell division (mitosis and meiosis), maintaining a constant body temperature (in endotherms), and nerve impulse transmission. The key misconception: plants DO respire — they respire 24/7, but during daylight hours, photosynthesis (which produces oxygen) usually masks respiration. At night, plants only respire, taking in oxygen and releasing CO₂.

illustration.alt: Diagram comparing breathing (ventilation) with cellular respiration, showing that respiration is a chemical reaction in cells releasing ATP.
illustration.caption: Breathing moves air in and out of lungs; respiration is the chemical release of ATP inside every living cell.

notes.heading: Aerobic Respiration
notes.body: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to fully break down glucose, releasing a large amount of energy. Word equation: Glucose + Oxygen → Carbon Dioxide + Water (+ energy). Balanced chemical equation: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O (+ energy as ATP). This process takes place in the mitochondria. It is the most efficient way to release energy — up to 38 ATP molecules per glucose molecule. Aerobic respiration occurs in most organisms most of the time. It requires a continuous supply of both glucose (from digestion or from starch/glycogen stores) and oxygen (from breathing or from photosynthesis). The carbon dioxide produced is a waste product — it diffuses out of cells into the blood (in animals) or into the air spaces in leaves (in plants) and is eventually exhaled or released through stomata. Water is either used by the body or excreted. Testing for respiration: CO₂ turns limewater cloudy/milky. This can be used in experiments to show that living organisms produce CO₂ during respiration (e.g., blow through a straw into limewater, or place germinating seeds in a sealed container with limewater).

illustration.alt: Diagram showing the aerobic respiration equation and a mitochondrion inside a cell.
illustration.caption: Aerobic respiration happens in mitochondria and releases up to 38 ATP per glucose.

notes.heading: Anaerobic Respiration in Animals
notes.body: Anaerobic respiration occurs when oxygen supply is insufficient for aerobic respiration — typically during strenuous exercise when muscles cannot receive enough oxygen. It releases energy from glucose without using oxygen, but produces far less ATP (only 2 ATP per glucose molecule). Word equation (in animals): Glucose → Lactic Acid (+ small amount of energy). No carbon dioxide is produced in animal anaerobic respiration. Lactic acid builds up in muscles, causing muscle fatigue — a burning sensation and reduced ability to contract. After exercise, lactic acid must be broken down. It is transported in the blood to the liver, where it is oxidised back to glucose (requiring oxygen). This is why we continue breathing heavily after exercise — the extra oxygen is needed to break down the accumulated lactic acid. This is called the oxygen debt (or EPOC — Excess Post-exercise Oxygen Consumption). Anaerobic respiration is a short-term emergency measure — it cannot sustain activity for long because (1) it is inefficient (produces little ATP) and (2) lactic acid accumulation becomes toxic to muscle cells.

illustration.alt: Diagram showing a muscle cell producing lactic acid during anaerobic respiration and repaying oxygen debt.
illustration.caption: Animal cells switch to lactic acid fermentation when oxygen cannot keep up with demand.

notes.heading: Anaerobic Respiration in Plants and Yeast
notes.body: Plants and yeast (a unicellular fungus) also carry out anaerobic respiration when oxygen is scarce — but the products are different from animals. Word equation (in plants and yeast): Glucose → Ethanol + Carbon Dioxide (+ small amount of energy). This process is called fermentation or alcoholic fermentation. It is economically important: (1) Bread-making — yeast in dough respires anaerobically, producing CO₂ bubbles that cause the dough to rise (the ethanol evaporates during baking). (2) Brewing and wine-making — yeast ferments sugars in barley (beer) or grapes (wine), producing ethanol. The CO₂ makes drinks fizzy. (3) Biofuel production — fermentation of sugar crops (sugar cane, corn) produces ethanol used as a renewable fuel. Key difference to remember: Animals produce LACTIC ACID. Plants and yeast produce ETHANOL + CO₂. Another difference: in waterlogged soil, plant roots may be forced into anaerobic respiration. The ethanol produced can be toxic, which is why most plants cannot survive prolonged flooding. Rice is an exception — it is adapted to transport oxygen to its roots.

illustration.alt: Diagram of yeast fermentation producing ethanol and carbon dioxide, used in bread and brewing.
illustration.caption: Yeast fermentation produces ethanol and CO₂ — essential for bread, beer and wine.

notes.heading: Comparing Aerobic and Anaerobic Respiration
notes.body: Both aerobic and anaerobic respiration release energy from glucose, but they differ in several key ways: (1) Oxygen requirement — aerobic needs oxygen; anaerobic does not. (2) Site — aerobic occurs in mitochondria; anaerobic occurs in the cytoplasm. (3) Energy yield — aerobic produces ~38 ATP per glucose; anaerobic only produces 2 ATP. (4) Products — aerobic produces CO₂ + H₂O; anaerobic in animals produces lactic acid; anaerobic in plants/yeast produces ethanol + CO₂. (5) Duration — aerobic can continue indefinitely (as long as oxygen and glucose are supplied); anaerobic is short-term (lactic acid or ethanol accumulation becomes toxic). (6) Completeness — aerobic completely oxidises glucose (all bonds broken); anaerobic partially breaks down glucose (lactic acid and ethanol still contain energy that could be released). Analogy: aerobic respiration is like a slow-burning log fire releasing all the energy; anaerobic is like a quick flash of flame releasing only a fraction of the energy and leaving behind unburnt fuel.

illustration.alt: Comparison table of aerobic and anaerobic respiration showing oxygen use, products, ATP yield and duration.
illustration.caption: Aerobic respiration is efficient and complete; anaerobic is fast but leaves energy in waste products.

notes.heading: Practical: Investigating Respiration
notes.body: Several simple experiments demonstrate respiration: (1) CO₂ production by living organisms — set up two boiling tubes connected by delivery tubes: one with germinating seeds (respiring), one with limewater. As seeds respire, the CO₂ produced bubbles through limewater, turning it cloudy/milky. A control uses boiled (dead) seeds. This can also be done with maggots, woodlice, or sprouting beans. (2) Heat production by germinating seeds — two vacuum flasks, one with germinating seeds and one with boiled seeds (control). Place a thermometer in each. The germinating seeds' flask shows a temperature rise due to the exothermic respiration reaction. (3) Effect of temperature on respiration — using respirometers or simply counting CO₂ bubbles from yeast/sugar solutions at different temperatures. Results follow an enzyme activity curve: rate increases with temperature to an optimum (~37°C for yeast), then drops sharply as enzymes denature. (4) Demonstrating oxygen consumption — a simple respirometer using a capillary tube with a drop of coloured liquid. As the organism (e.g., germinating seeds) respires, it consumes O₂ (and KOH/NaOH absorbs the CO₂ produced), reducing gas volume and pulling the liquid drop along the capillary.

illustration.alt: Diagram of a simple respirometer with germinating seeds and a moving coloured liquid drop.
illustration.caption: Oxygen consumption lowers pressure in the chamber, pulling the drop towards the seeds.

notes.heading: Respiration in the Body: Gas Exchange and the Role of Blood
notes.body: Respiration and gas exchange are linked but distinct. Gas exchange (breathing/ventilation) brings O₂ into the lungs and removes CO₂. Respiration is the cellular process using O₂ to release energy. The link: (1) Oxygen enters blood at alveoli, binds to haemoglobin in red blood cells → transported to all body cells → used in aerobic respiration in mitochondria. (2) CO₂ (waste product of aerobic respiration) diffuses out of cells into blood plasma → transported to lungs → diffuses into alveoli → exhaled. (3) Glucose (fuel) is absorbed from digested food in the small intestine → transported in blood plasma → taken up by cells. (4) Lactic acid (from anaerobic respiration) is transported from muscles to the liver via blood → oxidised back to glucose. During exercise, breathing rate and depth increase (more O₂ in, more CO₂ out), and heart rate increases (faster blood circulation to deliver O₂ and glucose and remove CO₂ and lactic acid). This is coordinated by the brain (medulla oblongata), which detects increased CO₂ levels in blood and signals the respiratory muscles to work harder. This integrates the respiratory, circulatory, muscular, and nervous systems.

illustration.alt: Schematic diagram showing oxygen, carbon dioxide, glucose and lactic acid transport between the lungs, blood, body cells, small intestine and liver.
illustration.caption: Blood transports O₂ from lungs to cells and CO₂ back, while glucose from the gut and lactic acid from muscles travel in the blood.

flashcards.definition: Respiration using oxygen to fully break down glucose into CO₂ and water, releasing a large amount of ATP energy (~38 per glucose).
flashcards.example: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O (+ energy). Most organisms respire aerobically most of the time.

flashcards.definition: Respiration without oxygen; glucose is partially broken down into lactic acid with a small ATP yield (only 2 per glucose).
flashcards.example: During a sprint, muscles switch to anaerobic respiration when oxygen delivery cannot keep up with demand.

flashcards.definition: Anaerobic respiration in plants and yeast producing ethanol, CO₂, and a small amount of energy.
flashcards.example: Yeast ferments sugar into ethanol and CO₂ — used for making bread (CO₂ makes it rise) and alcoholic drinks (ethanol).

flashcards.definition: The organelle where aerobic respiration occurs. Often called the 'powerhouse' of the cell.
flashcards.example: Cells with high energy demands — like muscle cells, sperm cells, and ciliated cells — contain many mitochondria.

flashcards.definition: Adenosine triphosphate — the energy currency of the cell. Energy released from glucose during respiration is stored as ATP for immediate use.
flashcards.example: ATP provides energy for muscle contraction, active transport, protein synthesis, and cell division.

flashcards.definition: The waste product of anaerobic respiration in animals. Accumulates in muscles during intense exercise, causing fatigue and cramping.
flashcards.example: After a sprint, heavy breathing (oxygen debt) provides the oxygen needed to break down lactic acid in the liver.

flashcards.definition: The extra oxygen required after exercise to oxidise accumulated lactic acid back to glucose in the liver.
flashcards.example: You continue to breathe heavily for several minutes after finishing a 100-metre sprint — you are repaying the oxygen debt.

flashcards.definition: Limewater (calcium hydroxide solution) turns cloudy/milky in the presence of CO₂. Used to demonstrate that respiration produces CO₂.
flashcards.example: Blowing exhaled air through a straw into limewater turns it milky, showing that exhaled air contains CO₂ from respiration.

flashcards.definition: A chemical reaction that releases energy in the form of heat. Respiration is exothermic — this is why germinating seeds generate warmth.
flashcards.example: In a vacuum flask, germinating peas are warmer than boiled peas because their respiration releases heat energy.

flashcards.definition: A large, insoluble polysaccharide made of linked glucose molecules; the main carbohydrate storage molecule in animals (stored in liver and muscles).
flashcards.example: Between meals, glycogen is broken down into glucose to supply cells with fuel for respiration.

flashcards.definition: An apparatus used to measure the rate of respiration by tracking oxygen consumption or CO₂ production.
flashcards.example: A simple respirometer uses a capillary tube with a coloured liquid drop; as the organism consumes O₂, the drop moves towards the organism.

flashcards.definition: NOT the same as respiration. Ventilation is the physical movement of air into and out of the lungs. Respiration is the chemical release of energy inside cells.
flashcards.example: Inhalation brings O₂ into the lungs; respiration uses that O₂ inside mitochondria to produce ATP.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between breathing (ventilation) and respiration?
choices: They are the same thing — the terms are interchangeable
Breathing is the physical movement of air in and out of lungs; respiration is the chemical release of energy from glucose inside cells
Breathing happens only in animals; respiration only in plants
Breathing requires oxygen; respiration does not
questions.explanation: Ventilation is the mechanical process of moving air. Respiration is a chemical reaction (C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O) occurring in every living cell to release ATP energy.

questions.stem: Which word equation correctly describes aerobic respiration?
choices: Carbon dioxide + Water → Glucose + Oxygen
Glucose + Oxygen → Carbon dioxide + Water (+ energy)
Glucose → Lactic acid (+ energy)
Glucose → Ethanol + Carbon dioxide (+ energy)
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to break down glucose, producing CO₂, water, and a large amount of ATP energy. The other equations describe photosynthesis or anaerobic respiration.

questions.stem: During a 100-metre sprint, why do athletes' muscles switch to anaerobic respiration?
choices: Aerobic respiration stops working above a certain speed
Oxygen delivery to muscles cannot keep up with the very high energy demand, so the faster (but less efficient) anaerobic pathway is used
Sprinters' muscles do not contain mitochondria
Anaerobic respiration produces more ATP than aerobic
questions.explanation: During intense, short-duration exercise, the circulatory system cannot deliver oxygen fast enough to meet demand. Anaerobic respiration provides rapid ATP production, but only ~2 ATP per glucose vs ~38 aerobically.

questions.stem: What causes muscle fatigue during intense exercise?
choices: Depletion of oxygen in the atmosphere
Build-up of lactic acid from anaerobic respiration, which lowers pH and interferes with muscle contraction
Overproduction of carbon dioxide
Muscles running out of glucose completely
questions.explanation: Lactic acid accumulation increases acidity in muscle cells, inhibiting enzyme activity and muscle fibre contraction — this is experienced as the 'burn' and eventual inability to continue.

questions.stem: Yeast is used in bread-making because it produces CO₂ during anaerobic respiration. What does the CO₂ do?
choices: It gives bread its flavour
It forms bubbles that make the dough rise, creating a light, spongy texture
It kills bacteria in the dough
It converts starch into sugar
questions.explanation: Yeast ferments sugars in the dough, producing CO₂ gas. The gas bubbles get trapped in the elastic gluten network, causing the dough to expand and rise — creating the soft texture of bread.

questions.stem: A student breathes out through a straw into limewater. The limewater turns milky. What does this prove?
choices: Exhaled air contains more oxygen than inhaled air
Exhaled air contains carbon dioxide, a product of respiration
Exhaled air contains water vapour from respiration
Limewater reacts with oxygen in exhaled air
questions.explanation: Limewater (calcium hydroxide) reacts with CO₂ to form insoluble calcium carbonate, which appears as a milky/cloudy precipitate. This shows that respiring cells produce CO₂.

questions.stem: Why do plants NOT photosynthesise at night, but DO respire?
choices: Photosynthesis requires light, which is absent at night; respiration does not require light and happens continuously in all living cells
Plants switch between photosynthesis and respiration — they never do both
At night plants respire using stored starch instead of glucose
Plants only respire when they are growing
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis is light-dependent. Respiration is a continuous process in all living cells, 24/7, to provide energy for maintenance. At night, plants take in O₂ and release CO₂ — they are respiring.

questions.stem: What is the 'oxygen debt' and why does it occur?
choices: The amount of oxygen the body owes to the lungs after holding one's breath
The extra oxygen needed after exercise to oxidise lactic acid back to glucose in the liver
The oxygen that muscles store for future use
The oxygen consumed during anaerobic respiration
questions.explanation: After anaerobic exercise, accumulated lactic acid must be removed. The liver uses oxygen to convert lactic acid back into glucose — this requires extra oxygen beyond normal resting levels, hence the 'debt' repaid by continued heavy breathing.

questions.stem: Which product is formed ONLY during anaerobic respiration in plants and yeast, but NOT in animals?
choices: Lactic acid
Carbon dioxide
Ethanol
Water
questions.explanation: Plants and yeast produce ethanol + CO₂ during anaerobic respiration (fermentation). Animals produce lactic acid only (no CO₂ in animal anaerobic respiration).

questions.stem: Where in the cell does aerobic respiration occur?
choices: Cytoplasm
Nucleus
Mitochondria
Ribosomes
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration takes place in the mitochondria. Anaerobic respiration occurs in the cytoplasm (glycolysis only).

questions.stem: Two vacuum flasks contain seeds: Flask A has germinating seeds; Flask B has boiled (dead) seeds. After 24 hours, Flask A is warmer. Why?
choices: Germinating seeds absorb more heat from the surroundings
Respiration is an exothermic reaction — the germinating seeds release heat energy as they respire
Boiled seeds reflect heat better
Dead seeds absorb the heat produced by live seeds
questions.explanation: Respiration is exothermic — it releases energy as heat. Germinating seeds respire rapidly, generating measurable warmth. Boiled seeds are dead and do not respire, so no heat is produced.

questions.stem: Why can a human only sprint at maximum speed for a short period?
choices: The heart gets tired and stops beating
Anaerobic respiration is inefficient — it produces little ATP and lactic acid builds up, causing muscle fatigue
Aerobic respiration stops working after 10 seconds
The lungs run out of oxygen storage
questions.explanation: Maximum sprinting relies heavily on anaerobic respiration, which yields only ~2 ATP per glucose (vs ~38 aerobically). Lactic acid accumulation rapidly causes fatigue, limiting sprint duration to seconds.

questions.stem: Which gas is consumed during aerobic respiration?
choices: Carbon dioxide
Nitrogen
Oxygen
Hydrogen
questions.explanation: Oxygen is the reactant in aerobic respiration that acts as the final electron acceptor, enabling the complete breakdown of glucose.

questions.stem: A mouse is placed in a sealed respirometer. Soda lime (absorbs CO₂) is in the chamber. The coloured liquid drop moves TOWARDS the mouse. What does this show?
choices: The mouse is producing more CO₂ than it consumes O₂
The mouse is consuming O₂ for respiration; CO₂ is absorbed by soda lime, so the total gas volume decreases, pulling the drop inward
The mouse is photosynthesising
The temperature change is pushing the drop
questions.explanation: Respiration consumes O₂ and produces CO₂. If CO₂ is absorbed by soda lime, the only net change is O₂ depletion — reducing gas volume in the chamber and pulling the liquid drop towards the organism.

questions.stem: After a marathon, an athlete's blood contains less lactic acid than after a 400-metre sprint. Why?
choices: Marathon runners produce no lactic acid
Marathons are run at a pace where oxygen delivery keeps up with demand — mostly aerobic respiration — so little lactic acid accumulates. Sprinting exceeds oxygen supply, relying on anaerobic
Sweating removes lactic acid during the marathon
Lactic acid is converted to CO₂ during long-distance running
questions.explanation: Long-distance events are primarily aerobic — the steady pace allows the circulatory system to deliver enough oxygen to muscles. Sprints demand energy faster than oxygen can be supplied, triggering anaerobic respiration and lactic acid build-up.
